newsitem.title: HUNGARY: HUNGARY TOP MKT PERFORMER IN CENTRAL EUROPE - HSBC.
newsitem.headline: HUNGARY TOP MKT PERFORMER IN CENTRAL EUROPE - HSBC.

text.p: Central Europe as a region offers very good investment chances in 1997, but overall, the Hungarian market has the greatest potential, HSBC James Capel said in its latest market research, dated February 3.

"Helped by good growth prospects in the domestic economies, attractive valuations and an inflow of foreign capital, we see the region as a whole providing excellent investment opportunities," emerging market strategist Nigel Rendell said.
"We believe that the Hungarian market has the greatest potential with the BUX forecast to reach 7,500 by year-end - generating a U.S. dollar return for the year of 50 percent."
In a bull run the BUX index surged to 5,572.80 points on February 3, from 4,134.31 points at the end of last year.
Rendell said the market should be boosted by the recovery in the domestic economy, with the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) rising by an estimated three percent this year.

Further cuts in short-term interest rates, declining inflation and reasonable valuation will also bolster the Budapest market, he said. "Parliamentary elections in springs 1998 should not dent investor enthusiasm."
The Polish market also has good outlook, but higher money market rates could limit the gains, Rendell said.
"In Poland the performance of the market should also be good, but gains may be held back by the recent hikes in money market rates," he said.
"We see little chance of interest rates providing a more favourable backdrop until domestic growth has started to moderate."
Rendell said Polish corporate earnings growth should be reasonable and on a 1997 price/earnings ratio of 10.5 the market is not expensive.
HSBC James Capel's December 1997 target for the WIG of 21,000 points represented a close to 30 percent gain for the dollar-based investor.
The Czech market is lagging behind with a more modest gains forecast "given the concerns about liquidity and the growing current account deficit," Rendell said.
"We see the PX50 reaching 650 by end-1997, implying a 15 percent dollar return during the year."
